items.title: Yanliang Miao is right that it would be a mistake to assume that China’s economy is running out of steam simply because property and infrastructure i...
items.description_html:
Yanliang Miao is right that it would be a mistake to assume that China’s economy is running out of steam simply because property and infrastructure investment are weakening.

But I disagree with his suggestion that China can largely replace the old investment-driven growth model with a technology-driven one as it rebalances toward domestic demand. The problem is that China’s extraordinary technological competitiveness is itself mostly a consequence of the imbalances that created the old model.

China’s challenge, in other words, is not simply to find new engines of growth by continuing to fund technological progress in the same way it has in the past. It is to develop new engines of growth even as surging debt and growing international tensions force it to reverse the very conditions that created its past technological progress – excessively high investment and excessively low consumption.

This was the same challenge the USSR faced in the 1960s and Japan in the 1980s, and neither was able to do so. Their failure was not an accident. As with China today, it was precisely their highly unbalanced economies that funded their spectacular technological advances until debt capacity limits forced a reversal.

That’s the problem. Until it figures out how to maintain technological progress while dramatically restructuring the conditions that created it in the past, Beijing will continue to try to “solve” the supply-side “problem” China doesn’t have while worsening the real constraint on its economy, its unbalanced demand.
https://www.imf.org/en/publications/fandd/issues/2026/09/chinas-emerging-economic-engine-yanliang-miao

items.title: Caixin: "China has unveiled a sweeping five-year plan for its electronic information manufacturing sector, aiming to boost the industry’s annual reve...
items.description_html:
Caixin: "China has unveiled a sweeping five-year plan for its electronic information manufacturing sector, aiming to boost the industry’s annual revenue beyond 30 trillion yuan ($4.5 trillion) by 2030."

This is extraordinarily ambitious. There is no directly comparable global measure because China’s definition is unusually broad, encompassing everything from integrated circuits and advanced computing to consumer electronics and energy electronics. But global consumer-electronics manufacturing generated about $2.1 trillion in 2025, while global semiconductor sales were under $1 trillion.

China’s target therefore implies that it expects Chinese electronic-information manufacturing to account for an extraordinarily large share of global production by 2030.

This requires of course both that the massive expansion in its global share can occur without a collapse in profits, and that the the rest of the world (especially East Asia, where much of the production is currently concentrated) is willing to accommodate the Chinese target by giving up its own share of production.
https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-09-17/china-targets-45-trillion-tech-manufacturing-sector-by-2030-102485603.html?cxg=web&Sfrom=twitter

items.description_html:
"It would be surprising if the Tata Sons board simply acquiesced to the RBI. Five of its six current directors were on the board in 2024 and were ostensibly against listing, without which the company would not have moved to deregister itself. The group doyen Ratan Tata was alive then and his desire to keep the holding company private is widely known. Noel Tata, who has taken Ratan’s place as chairman of the trusts and joined the Tata Sons board, is also reportedly opposed to a listing.

If the board turns course now, the obvious question is: What changed?

One possibility is the bitter internal politics that have since engulfed the group, pitting Noel Tata versus Chandrasekaran.

Another possibility is simpler: the board may not have the stomach for lengthy litigation against a powerful regulator.

Few have taken on the RBI. Veteran banker Uday Kotak did, challenging its ownership rules for banks before eventually reaching a settlement and withdrawing the case.

A court battle may not deliver Tata Sons the answer it wants either, as Parekh noted earlier. Even a successful challenge could merely result in the matter being sent back to the regulator for reconsideration."

items.title: RT menaka doshi: How India’s Local Art Scene Hit The Global Stage The Venice Biennale is known as the Olympics of the art world — roughly 100 countr...
items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
How India’s Local Art Scene Hit The Global Stage

The Venice Biennale is known as the Olympics of the art world — roughly 100 countries, along with many more museums, artists and foundations, put on exhibitions throughout the Italian city.

This year there was no escaping the omnipresence of India during the festival’s opening in May.

“Today there is much greater confidence. Indian collectors are buying more thoughtfully, galleries are more ambitious, institutions are stronger, and artists are increasingly part of international exhibitions and museum collections.” - Jaya Asokan.

“India is at the cultural center of the world right now. Fashion, music, art — it’s all being appreciated at scale.” - Atelier Ashiesh Shah

“The wealthier people in India have finally accepted the fact that the best legacy they can leave behind is art and culture.” - Dinesh Vazirani, Saffronart

Vazarini recalls a foreign buyer visiting Saffronart’s gallery a few decades ago and asking about a piece by S.H. Raza, a renowned abstract painter. It was priced at $10,000. “He said, ‘Call me when it’s $200,000,’ ” Vazirani says. “Art builds gravitas with value. That’s when people start taking it seriously.”

Raza’s top auction price is now $6.3 million; his work has sold for more than $1 million 38 times, according to the Artnet price database.

items.title: 7 mental models you must learn as a new budding investor: 1. Relative strength for thematic and industry spotting. 2. Spotting growth rates of a compa...
items.description_html:
7 mental models you must learn as a new budding investor:

1. Relative strength for thematic and industry spotting.

2. Spotting growth rates of a company: knowing how to read topline and bottom like growth + results of a co.

3. Learning how to spot rate of change and the growth catalyst.

4. Scanning for high volume names where something is changing fundamentally in the business. @stockscansin can help here :)

5. Learn about how to differentiate between a commodity business and one of a kind. Tailwinds in both can lead to different outcomes in terms of valuations and what market wants to pay.

6. Learn an entry/exit system using basic TA or FA. Stage analysis and understanding earnings downgrade/upgrade cycle should help you. Understand how market environment plays a role in supercharging your returns. Learn from the previous bull/bear markets.

7. Analyse businesses from first principles. Avoid the obvious Frauds and distill down your thesis into key track able KPIs.

Most important, track your PF performance from time to time vs all the major indices.

What does the 2026 BRICS summit mean for the Global South, and how is the bloc shaping cooperation on climate, trade and sustainable development?

The 18th BRICS Leaders’ Summit, hosted by India in New Delhi on September 12–13, placed climate change, finance, trade and global value chains among the key issues under its theme of ‘Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.’

The New Delhi Declaration reaffirmed the importance of multilateralism and called for greater support for developing countries on climate finance and adaptation. It also raised concerns over unilateral trade measures, including carbon border adjustment mechanisms, while advancing cooperation on global value chains.

items.title: The peptide market: $51 Bn TAM, on its way to $100 Bn by FY34. The pipeline went from ~100 molecules to 800 in development. Semaglutide alone is a $24...
items.description_html:
The peptide market: $51 Bn TAM, on its way to $100 Bn by FY34. The pipeline went from ~100 molecules to 800 in development. Semaglutide alone is a $24 Bn drug.

But here's the part that matters throughout the value chain

A peptide is made on an 8-step assembly line: synthesise the amino acids -> anchor them to a bead -> add one link at a time -> cleave -> purify -> freeze-dry -> fill into a pen. Making the peptide is cheap. Anyone can string amino acids together.

The whole moat sits at Step 6: purification. It's slow, it's the hardest capability to build, and it's where the value quietly concentrates.

So who captures it?

-> Upstream (Aminos Acids): commodity building blocks, thin margins but steady.
-> Midstream CDMOs (synthesis + purification): 20-30%+ EBITDA, customer switching takes 2-3 years to re-qualify. This is the sweet spot.
-> Downstream (Dr. Reddy's, Sun, Zydus + Shaily's pen-device near-monopoly in India): highest absolute margins, but generics compress them over time.

The number to internalise: an FDA-inspected peptide purification line with 3+ commercial programs takes a rival 5+ years and $100M+ to replicate.
The largest position is rarely the most durable one. The one that's hardest to copy is.

items.title: Exchanges should be the classic EM compounder: healthy growth, fat margins, 40%+ ROE. But Indian exchanges are not a market-expansion story. They are ...
items.description_html:
Exchanges should be the classic EM compounder: healthy growth, fat margins, 40%+ ROE.

But Indian exchanges are not a market-expansion story.

They are a retail speculator P&L, built on options trading.

Thats the whole earnings model:
> Retail scaled up
> Earnings inflected
> Multiples expanded
> Stock returns went vertical

Great businesses, yes but volatility is a friend of these exchanges. If we compare the 2 listed exchanges in India one commodity and one equity both are portraying completely different picture here.

Same month (Aug-26):
> MCX options contracts: 4.3x YoY, and still up 2% MoM
> BSE premium ADTO: down 22%

The equity options wave that built BSE is maturing: VIX at 11.2 (all-time low), STT hike on futures, RBI's tighter leverage norms on prop desks, and now CAS uncertainty on expiry days.

Meanwhile commodity derivatives are where equity derivatives were 3-4 years ago:

> Only 25% of equity F&O traders have touched MCX (was 12% in FY25)
> Commodity options are less than 5% of equity option contracts, less than 1% by premium

JLL's Sept 2026 numbers:
• Capacity today: 1.6 GW, aiming for 6 GW by 2029
• H1 2026 new capacity delivered: 85 MW
• H1 2026 absorption: 101 MW
• Vacancy: 2.8%, a record low

I think reaching 6 GW needs about 1.25 GW a year from here. At the H1 pace, India is adding around 170 MW a year, roughly one seventh of what's needed. So demand is taking up space faster than it gets built. Power connections and transformer lead times are still the real bottlenecks.

items.title: Performance should be measured by whether the earnings thesis plays out, not by whether the stock price happens to be depressed or elevated. That came...
items.description_html:
Performance should be measured by whether the earnings thesis plays out, not by whether the stock price happens to be depressed or elevated.

That came from someone whose portfolio has compounded at roughly 50% CAGR, uninterrupted, over the last 7-8 years.

Our portfolios could hardly be more different.

He had the foresight to get into several PSU and defence names early. I took a very different path. We have known each other since the 1990s, yet it is rare for our top 10 holdings to overlap.

We also rarely arrive at the same conclusion.

And that is precisely the point.

A portfolio should be aligned with your inner system, not with social validation.

You need to be able to own something when the person sitting next to you doesn't understand why you own it.

You need to be comfortable being wrong without immediately assuming that the other person must be right.

Markets don't require us to agree with each other.

They require us to know why we own what we own, what would prove the thesis right, and what would make us change our mind.

Different portfolios. Different mental models. Different paths.

And that is perfectly fine.

items.title: Congratulations to Ravi ji on the well-deserved recognition as CFO of the Year 2026, Best Returns (Large Cap). @LaurusLabs Cast your mind back to Laur...
items.description_html:
Congratulations to Ravi ji on the well-deserved recognition as CFO of the Year 2026, Best Returns (Large Cap). @LaurusLabs

Cast your mind back to Laurus Labs' FY23 earnings call in April 2023.

Arun from Nuvama was questioning the CDMO numbers and the heavy investment being made. Strip out the one large order, he argued, and CDMO looked stuck, while thousands of crores of capex sat at 50–60% utilisation. He then made a simple point on guidance: with so many investors listening, management should have some margin of safety.

Ravi ji replied:

"We also know the margin of safety."

Looking back, I don't think either side was wrong.

Arun was on the analyst's clock: guidance, estimates, actuals, accountability. That clock runs quarter to quarter, and it has to.

He was right to hold management to what it had actually said. The $1 billion ambition had already been revised. On the same call, management said FY24 would be flattish and that EBITDA margins would not go below 20–21%.

The problem with giving numbers is simple. Once you give them, you accept the scoreboard.

And FY24 missed it. Revenue fell 17%, and EBITDA margin came in at 15.8%, well below the floor management had discussed. On the analyst's clock, that was a clear miss.

Management was on a longer clock: capacity, capabilities, customers, commercialisation.

That clock moves slowly.

Build the capability first. Then fill the capacity. Then deepen customer relationships. Then let the economics show up.

The transcript shows management was already running on it. They wouldn't say how many CDMO projects would commercialise or when. But they were willing to put around ₹800 crore into synthesis, because they said they had visibility on what to make, how much to make and whom to sell to. They also expensed pre-operative costs rather than capitalising them, which made near-term margins look worse, not better.

They were uncertain about timing, but confident about direction.

FY26 showed what that was building: revenue of ₹6,813 crore, EBITDA margin of 26.8%, and CDMO revenue above ₹2,000 crore, this time from a broader base rather than one large order.

And Ravi ji had something an analyst doesn't: soul in the game.

"Don't judge me today, I'm building for tomorrow" is easy to say. A promoter-CFO with a large part of his wealth tied to the business has a very different relationship with the words "margin of safety". The claim costs him something if he's wrong.

That deserves to be taken seriously. It still deserves to be tested.

So the lesson from that 2023 exchange isn't that Ravi ji eventually won and Arun lost.

Arun wasn't an obstacle to the long game. He was part of its feedback loop. The long clock can't be judged without periodically checking the short one.

Both sides carry a warning.

A long-horizon manager still has to survive the short rounds. Otherwise "long term" becomes an unfalsifiable shield.

An analyst shouldn't confuse a bad year with a broken business. Otherwise every period of heavy investment looks like a failure.

The investor's job sits between the two.

Ask Arun's question: what did you promise, and did you deliver? Then ask Ravi ji, 'What are you building that today's numbers don't yet capture?'

Two clocks. Neither side had to be wrong.

Disclosure: I have been long Laurus since around 3500 crore market cap (Dec 2019 entry). None of this is investment advice or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold the stock. Please do your own work.

🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame.

Here’s how it works:

→ Prepaid order gets “cancelled” without the customer or brand knowing

→ Brand gets charged two-way delivery fees for an order nobody cancelled

→ Small items get shipped back in oversized boxes to inflate the RTO cost

→ Customer calls in confused: “I never cancelled this, I was waiting for it”

The brand loses the product, the shipping cost, the RTO cost, and the customer relationship. In one transaction.

Every D2C founder in India has lived this. Not once. On repeat.

And the wildest part? This is a multi thousand crore leak across the industry and almost nobody is building to fix it. 🤷🏻‍♂️

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.title: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely...
items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.description_html: Earnings growth picture for Dec'25 quarter vs Dec'24 quarter. Wtd Avg (growth in sum total earnings) is significantly better for the mid and small cap universe. Small cap has an exceptional earnings from Kiri Ind with 5000 cr plus (vs 177 cr year ago) which skews the growth much higher than normal. If you remove that, the wtd avg growth is 14.9%. Median growth reduces influence of such outliers or exceptional items and hence gives a better directional picture. Over all growth is good but nothing exceptional. I believe we should see much improved growth in the Mar'26 quarter as sharp pick up in economic activity (as covered in my last memo) started in the month of December 2025.

items.title: As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/Mar...
items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight

items.title: As Indian Railways issues an RFI for a new generation of passenger locomotives, here’s a fascinating throwback to 1995. An Antonov An-124 in Melbourn...
items.description_html:
As Indian Railways issues an RFI for a new generation of passenger locomotives, here’s a fascinating throwback to 1995.

An Antonov An-124 in Melbourne, Australia, is loading some very special cargo destined for Switzerland:

The shell of an ABB-designed WAP-5 locomotive for Indian Railways. 🇮🇳🚆

The shell would first travel to Switzerland, where essential propulsion systems were fitted, before eventually making its way to India.

It was part of the initial batch of locomotives procured from ABB’s Australian and Swiss operations.

But the bigger story wasn’t just the locomotives India imported.

It was the technology and technical know-how that came with them.

That technology-transfer journey helped India absorb modern 3-phase electric locomotive technology and eventually build increasingly powerful locomotives domestically.

Three decades later, descendants of that technology—most notably the WAP-5, WAP-7, and WAG-9 families and newer derivatives—are everywhere on the Indian Railways network.

Sometimes a single photograph captures the beginning of a multi-decade technology journey.

items.description_html:
Tata Electronics has been at the forefront of the Indian semiconductor sector; it is setting up a $11bn fab in Gujarat for 28-110nm chips with PSMC of Taiwan.

Construction is underway, and Tata has entered into an MoU with ASML for lithography equipment, talent development and supply-chain collaboration for the facility.

It has also signed a strategic alliance with Intel to help build a broader silicon and compute ecosystem in India. The fab is designed for capacity of ~50,000 wafers/month, with trial production targeted following installation and qualification of equipment.

Tata Electronics, Himax Technologies of Taiwan, and PSMC have also signed a MoU to deliver end-to-end display semiconductor solutions from chip design to manufacturing and packaging, as well as electronics manufacturing services (EMS) for both Indian and global markets. Himax (HIMX US) is a fabless semiconductor design company, focused on display and imaging ICs, with ~40% global market share in automotive display drivers chips.

The three companies also plan to collaborate to design and manufacture next-generation display solutions to meet global demand while enhancing supply chain resilience. Tata has also signed an MoU with Fujifilm of Japan to establish semiconductor materials ecosystem in India

Construction at Tata's ~$3bn OSAT facility in Assam is progressing, with production expected to commence during FY27. The facility is designed to package ~48mn chips/day using advanced packaging technologies, including flip-chip and Integrated System in-Package (ISIP), for automotive, EV, telecom and consumer electronics applications.

Tata Electronics has signed a partnership with Qualcomm to manufacture Qualcomm automotive modules in India, while L&T Semiconductor Technologies has announced plans to shift backend semiconductor operations to India and leverage Tata Electronics' assembly and packaging infrastructure.

items.title: Emkay on MDR - NPCI announces MDR on UPI – Paytm, Pine Labs to benefit MDR on UPI – Key takeaways The 0.4% MDR is capped at Rs 300 for transactions ...
items.description_html:
Emkay on MDR -

NPCI announces MDR on UPI – Paytm, Pine Labs to benefit

MDR on UPI – Key takeaways

The 0.4% MDR is capped at Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 and above. Specified sectors (railways, telecom, insurance, fuel, and agricultural inputs), accounting for ~46% of UPI P2M transaction value, will pay a flat Rs5 per transaction for transaction value above Rs2,000.

Capital market payments (MFs, securities, and stockbroking/dealer transactions) attract a lower 0.02% MDR, also capped at Rs300, while small merchants receiving up to Rs100k/month via UPI QR codes under the P2PM classification continue to enjoy 0 MDR.

The framework applies only to direct account-to-merchant-account UPI transactions, excluding UPI-linked CC payments, and is expected to affect only ~4% of the overall merchant transaction volume.

NPCI introduced a 0.4% MDR on P2M transactions above Rs2,000 from 15-Oct-26, while leaving the mass market untouched — P2P transfers, sub-Rs2,000 tickets, and small P2PM merchants all remain free of charge, while select categories have lower MDR/capped per-transaction MDR.

While 67% of the P2M transactions by value are above Rs2,000, we expect a lower eligible GMV. The more important signal, in our view, is that UPI acquiring now carries a commercial revenue model that is contractual, recurring, and scales with value, in place of a discretionary annual subsidy.

This will make the payment business structurally self-sustaining, making the business model much more resilient. On conservative assumptions (ie 10bps/6bps realized take-rates for Paytm/Pine Labs), we estimate FY28 UPI MDR revenue of Rs11.2bn/Rs1.55bn, respectively.

The present value of this stream adds Rs434bn and Rs51.2bn to our valuations for Paytm and Pine Labs, increasing our TP to Rs2,400 and Rs230, respectively. We maintain BUY on both Paytm and Pine Labs

items.title: India's electric 2W story seems to be entering its next phase — from adoption to serious scale. Look at what is happening across the industry: → Ult...
items.description_html:
India's electric 2W story seems to be entering its next phase — from adoption to serious scale.

Look at what is happening across the industry:

→ Ultraviolette is investing ₹779 Cr in a new Hosur facility — 2.5 lakh units initial capacity, scalable to 5 lakh units.

→ Ather is building its new Aurangabad facility with planned capacity of up to 10 lakh units. Management has said supply constraints were costing it potentially 13,000–15,000 scooter sales every month.

→ TVS sold ~49,000 electric 2Ws in August retail, nearly +91% YoY, commanding ~27% market share. Company-reported EV sales were even higher at 59,453 units, +137% YoY.

→ Bajaj Chetak sold 3.03 lakh units in FY26 and crossed 7 lakh cumulative sales. In August, Bajaj retailed ~41,000 EV 2Ws and had ~22% market share.

→ Eicher/Royal Enfield has finally entered EVs through Flying Flea. The C6 is already on sale, although management is deliberately taking a slow city-by-city approach rather than chasing volumes immediately.

→ BGauss is also scaling rapidly — August sales were ~4,845 units, up ~180% YoY.

And the bigger number:

India sold ~1.83 lakh electric 2Ws in August alone, +67% YoY.

EV penetration has moved from 7.7% in Aug-25 to ~10.7% in Aug-26, after crossing 11% in July.

TVS. Bajaj. Ather. Hero. Eicher. Ultraviolette. BGauss.

Everyone is investing, launching products and adding capacity.

The EV 2W story is no longer just about startups disrupting incumbents.

The incumbents themselves are now going all-in.

The next battle will be about scale, distribution, product breadth, localisation and profitability.

The acquisition aims to create one of the largest integrated explosives and blasting solutions platforms globally. Omnia operates in 23 countries with over 70 distribution centres, serving customers in more than 40 countries including Australia, the United States, Canada, Brazil, and Indonesia.

A key component of the deal is Omnia’s integrated manufacturing infrastructure, including nitric acid and ammonium nitrate production facilities. Omnia recently doubled its ammonium nitrate storage capacity with a new 5,000-tonne storage tank. These assets are expected to enhance vertical integration and supply security for Solar’s explosives value chain.

Following the completing of this transaction, Omnia will be delisted from the Johannesburg Stock Exchange and A2X Markets securities exchange, the company said in its statement

In 2010, Solar Industries started its operations with the South African Development Community, establishing its first facility in Zambia.

According to Goldman Sachs, the proposed Omnia acquisition could strengthen Solar Industries' value chain in Africa while opening new geographies for the company.

items.description_html:
My latest report “The Ghost of Population Past: How Population Control Persists in India” (with @AakankshaArora5 & Virat). India's fertility rate is well below the replacement rate and some parts of the country now have East Asian/European fertility levels. The number of live births in India peaked in 2001 at 29 million and has now fallen below 23 million. Population growth is now driven by longevity improvements but the pipeline is shrinking. Yet, population control policies remain embedded in government policies even in those states that want to incentivise more children. This is similar to what happened in China where population control measures remained in place for decades after it was obvious that it causing demographic damage.

We would like clarify that we are not against family planning for reasons of health, child spacing or personal preference. The central argument of our paper is that population control is no longer relevant as an objective of state policy. Our family planning policies need to reflect the new demographic reality.

items.title: RT Ananth Rupanagudi: 1880s, a tea planter's house, Sibsagar, Assam! This photo illustrates the early era of British tea plantation architecture in No...
items.description_html:
RT Ananth Rupanagudi
1880s, a tea planter's house, Sibsagar, Assam! This photo illustrates the early era of British tea plantation architecture in Northeast India, long before the more uniform, brick-and-iron "Burra Bungalows" became standard across the region.

The building is a classic proto-type of the Chang Bungalow. This regional adaptation elevated the main living quarters onto raised wooden or bamboo stilts (chang). Raising the structure protected it from the severe seasonal monsoons and floods typical of the Brahmaputra Valley, while keeping it out of reach from wild animals and snakes.

Unlike later estate structures that utilized imported British iron frames, this early structure relies entirely on local materials. It features a steep, heavy thatched roof designed to quickly shed heavy rains, alongside woven bamboo wall panels (ikra) and a sturdy timber frame.

A deep, recessed upper-floor veranda provides shade to the interior rooms while facilitating excellent cross-ventilation. Decorative latticework and bamboo screens shade the upper balcony, filtering out glare while allowing the breeze to flow freely through the living space.

The photo depicts the lifestyle of the British colonial planters (Burra Sahibs). It shows horses being readied on a manicured lawn, framed by native trees. The planters are accompanied by local staff and attendants, capturing the sharp social division between the plantation management and the labour force that sustained the late-19th-century tea boom. #Assam #teaplanters #history

items.title: RT Nandini: Having read and thoroughly taken by @sanjeevsanyal’s The Revolutionaries, I was naturally very keen to see the web series on @PrimeVideo ...
items.description_html:
RT Nandini
Having read and thoroughly taken by @sanjeevsanyal’s The Revolutionaries, I was naturally very keen to see the web series on @PrimeVideo

To actually watch a book, its characters and the real-life personalities of such an important and tumultuous era of our history come alive on screen is something else altogether.

As the first episode unfolded, I found myself thinking about how little we really know of those extraordinary lives- lives that went against the tide of ordinary Indian citizenry that had largely accepted British rule as its lot and its future.

To risk life, limb and unimaginable torture at a time when the very idea of freedom was still nascent is almost impossible for us to comprehend today.

I also learnt many little details. The very details I have always believed our history books fail to tell us.

Details that make historical figures come alive and allow us to understand an era, rather than reducing history to a litany of dates, names and events.

Thank you, @nikhiladvani, for bringing this extraordinary canvas to life with your visual brush and @sanjeevsanyal for giving us the canvas in the first place.

On to Episode 2 tonight.

items.title: One argument to keep all transactions on UPI free because it's a small amount needs some reflection. Let me give an analogy. SCL was a fab that govern...
items.description_html:
One argument to keep all transactions on UPI free because it's a small amount needs some reflection.

Let me give an analogy. SCL was a fab that government ran. It started reasonably well but couldn't keep up because cutting-edge consumer and commercial tech requires constant capital re-investment which doesn't easily happen within governments.

Contrary to the story we are told that had it not been for the fire SCL would have been on top, the reality is that it had already fallen behind by the time that accident happened.

Similarly, I see that PSPs, TPAPs, NPCI all need to be viable businesses to continue to innovate on digital payments. In fact we should be having multiple NPCIs and interoperable protocols - something that the new umbrella entity policies of the RBI was trying. Our payments ecosystem is great in terms of scale but is falling behind like SCL from the frontier.

Get the private sector energy in or we will have another SCL like entity on our hands. And then we will again make some excuse.

items.title: RT Jesús Fernández-Villaverde: David Deutsch (@DavidDeutschOxf) has a nice post today explaining how he fixed his dishwasher with the help of ChatGP...
items.description_html:
RT Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
David Deutsch (@DavidDeutschOxf) has a nice post today explaining how he fixed his dishwasher with the help of ChatGPT. We have all been there over the last couple of years. In my case, from fixing a light fixture in my kitchen to repairing a leak in my irrigation system.

Deutsch and many readers point out something that has been a staple of my talks for a decade. GDP was designed to measure an economy that produced coal and steel, easily measurable quantities. And GDP did its job quite well for decades.

IT, first, and later the internet and AI, changed the landscape. My favorite example is books. Even as late as 2010 or so, getting the most recent books in Spanish on, let’s say, Spanish economic history was hard in the U.S.: expensive and time-consuming. Every time I went to Madrid, I carried two bags, one of them empty because it would come back filled with books. Then Kindle arrived, and now I can buy nearly every single Spanish book I want in seconds and at a lower price than the physical copy. This was an enormous increase in my welfare that never got reflected in GDP.

The literature is divided on how big this effect is. I tend to side with those who think it is a big deal. Therefore, many of the gains in GDP growth announced by the strongest defenders of AI might not materialize: they will go instead into higher welfare.

But the issue goes beyond getting GDP wrong. What Deutsch perhaps did not notice is that he did not pay VAT on the service of the repair person he did not hire, and that such a repair person did not pay income taxes on the service he did not render.

Taxing AI-based economies might thus become much harder, from a purely technical perspective. One solution would be to tax the profits of OpenAI (or Deutsch’s subscription), but I am among those who think those profits are not going to be nearly as large as anticipated. Competition among labs will drive the subscription prices of models down (unless labs can cartelize, for example, by appealing to “AI security”). Over 95%, and perhaps as much as 99%, of the gains from AI will pass to the final user, whether another business or an individual.

Now, we could tax the final user, for instance, at a fixed rate per token used. But that implies we are taxing the high-return activity (how to fix the dishwasher) at the same rate as the low-return activity (Claude: “tell me a joke about my cat jumping”). And taxing per token might hurt those final users who use more tokens because they are more productive, something we might not want to do (yes, there is something called the uniform commodity taxation theorem, but it often breaks down).

Let me give you an extreme example: imagine that tomorrow the new OpenAI model cures all cancers, forever. Just a vaccine, $10, once in your life, and you never get cancer again. The increase in human welfare from such an invention would be staggering. But how do you measure it in GDP? Yes, people will live longer, perhaps work longer. A second-order effect on GDP. And more importantly: how do you tax the vaccine? Do you even want to tax the vaccine? I would argue we want to subsidize it, and generously.

When I was still an undergrad, my first RA job was helping to construct GDP and other national aggregate statistics in Spain. It was a most valuable experience, because it made me aware of what GDP means, its strengths (and it has many more than its critics concede), and its limitations. But it also taught me that what you can tax out of GDP is far more limited than you would think at first sight.

There are real upper bounds on taxation, and I am afraid the bound is tighter now than it used to be.

items.title: Lots of very downbeat takes on Saudi oil. Yet, Riyadh exported yesterday ~6m barrels via Hormuz dark transits -- roughly half of what left the Persian...
items.description_html:
Lots of very downbeat takes on Saudi oil.

Yet, Riyadh exported yesterday ~6m barrels via Hormuz dark transits -- roughly half of what left the Persian Gulf on the day. Satellite data shows further tankers were loading yesterday at Ras Tanura and Juaymah.

If the kingdom wants, it can replicate UAE/Iraq/Kuwait SoH dark transits strategy. All what takes is political will (which Riyadh has been forced to find after an attack closed the East-West oil pipeline) and money to pay for incredible expensive freight.

Aramco has spent the last two days selling huge amounts of crude for delivery ship-to-ship in late Sept and Oct in the Gulf of Oman. Most going to Asia.

items.title: RT Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський: Ukraine has proposed that its partners secure an agreement with Russia that would st...
items.description_html:
RT Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський
Ukraine has proposed that its partners secure an agreement with Russia that would stop the destruction of critical infrastructure. Food, energy, and other basics that sustain life must be protected, and Russian strikes are directed primarily against them. Every day, Ukrainian energy facilities, port infrastructure, logistics, and even warehouses storing food and pharmaceuticals are targeted. Ukraine is not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by any agreement.

If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes. So that it is reliable, long-term, has a real impact on people’s lives, and does not fall apart after the Russians hold their “elections” and get an easing of pressure on gasoline and diesel precisely for that period. The war must be brought to an end. And a de-escalatory step regarding critical infrastructure could be the first step toward peace. We expect specifics from our partners.

items.description_html:
BREAKING: China acquired +35 tonnes of gold in July via the London OTC market, its 3rd-largest monthly purchase since mid-2025, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

This is 75% more than the official +20 tonnes reported by China's central bank for July.

This also follows estimated purchases of +48 and +40 tonnes through the OTC market in May and June, respectively.

This brings the total for these 3 months up to +123 tonnes.

By comparison, China’s central bank has officially increased its gold reserves by +80 tonnes in the first 8 months of the year.

China’s gold accumulation is far larger than its official figures reveal.

items.title: Is the 10Y Note Yield heading to 6.0%? Historically, the 10Y Note Yield has risen +50 basis points on average in the first 6 months after the Fed bega...
items.description_html:
Is the 10Y Note Yield heading to 6.0%?

Historically, the 10Y Note Yield has risen +50 basis points on average in the first 6 months after the Fed began hiking rates, across tightening cycles since 1963.

Over the following 12 months, the average increase reached +110 basis points.

If this materializes again, the 10Y Note Yield would surpass 6.0% next year for the first time since August 2000.

Meanwhile, the most extreme cases saw increases of up to +400 basis points in the 10Y Note Yield over the 12 months following the first hike.

On the other hand, some declines of up to -70 basis points were also recorded over the same period.

More US Treasury intervention is likely coming.

items.title: Today is another reminder of just how fast things can change. Just 9 months ago, markets were pricing in 3 rate cuts in 2026 and we had $60 oil prices...
items.description_html:
Today is another reminder of just how fast things can change.

Just 9 months ago, markets were pricing in 3 rate cuts in 2026 and we had $60 oil prices.

Today, a new Fed rate hike cycle has begun, oil prices are above $100, and diesel prices are at record highs.

The market and the Fed are in agreement, lower rates are not coming as long as the current energy crisis continues.

There simply is no scenario where rate cuts are warranted with $100+ oil prices and 3.5%+ inflation, aside from an economic depression.

Luckily, we are also in the midst of the biggest technological revolution in history, and the AI boom continues to provide substantial support for the S&P 500.

Without the AI Revolution, markets would be in a much darker position right now.

On the flip side, a resolution to the current energy crisis opens for the S&P 500 to rise well above 8,000.

For now, a long and bumpy road appears to be ahead as the Fed continues its 60-straight-month battle against inflation.

"Higher for longer" has returned.

items.title: The Fed made a very clear statement today. Not only did they hike interest rates, but it was a 12-0 unanimous decision. This marks the first unanimous...
items.description_html:
The Fed made a very clear statement today.

Not only did they hike interest rates, but it was a 12-0 unanimous decision.

This marks the first unanimous Fed decision since May 2025, amid calls from President Trump to cut rates.

And, the Fed concluded their policy statement by saying, "The Committee will deliver price stability," making it clear that inflation is their top priority.

The question now becomes: How does President Trump respond?

12 days ago, President Trump said he would "stop trading" with 50+ US trade partners if the Fed does not cut rates.

Today, the Fed not only avoided cutting rates, they hiked them.

Clearly, the divide between the White House and the Fed is widening, even with Jerome Powell out.

More to come.

items.title: Investors are no longer hedging against a tech stock crash. The average 1-month put-to-call skew of the Nasdaq 100 index is down to 0 points, its 4th-...
items.description_html:
Investors are no longer hedging against a tech stock crash.

The average 1-month put-to-call skew of the Nasdaq 100 index is down to 0 points, its 4th-lowest reading over the last 20 years.

This measures how much more investors are paying for downside protection through put options than for upside exposure through call options, with the current reading indicating historically low demand for Nasdaq put options.

This figure has dropped -0.25 points since March 2026, one of the largest 6-month declines on record.

By comparison, the long-term average of this metric is 0.11 points.

Meanwhile, the cost of options used to bet on or protect against large moves in the average Nasdaq 100 stock fell sharply last week, with 1-month implied volatility dropping -17 percentage points, to ~40%.

Investors are extremely bullish on tech.

items.title: The BRICS Summit headlines so far ! 1. Iran & UAE agreed to the same language on the Middle East war. Iran is a BRICS member while UAE is closely alig...
items.description_html:
The BRICS Summit headlines so far !

1. Iran & UAE agreed to the same language on the Middle East war. Iran is a BRICS member while UAE is closely aligned with the U.S. - so this is significant.

2. BRICS took a position clearly uncomfortable for the U.S. - the declaration criticises unilateral sanctions & tariff/non-tariff measures.. Basically says sanctions outside the UN framework should be eliminated.

3. India has tried to prevent BRICS becoming an anti-West bloc. PM Modi's formulation - "BRICS is not against anyone". This kind of also points to a more fundamental tension within the bloc - Russia & China are much more comfortable presenting it as a counterweight to Western power. India & Brazil not so much.

4. President Xi is in India for the first time in 7 years. PM Modi reiterated that peace on the border remains the essential basis for a normal relationship. The Modi-Xi bilateral may ultimately matter a lot.

5. Xi is trying to position China & BRICS as a peacemaker in the Iran conflict. He explicitly urged BRICS countries to play a peace-making role and said China was prepared to do its part.

6. President Putin has used the summit to reinforce the Russia-India relationship & his wider argument that Russia is not isolated. In his bilateral with Modi, the two reiterated the target of taking bilateral trade towards $100 billion by 2030.

7. There has been a significant absence - no dramatic 'BRICS currency' moment. This is worth stressing because headlines around BRICS often overstate de-dollarization.

#BRICS #IranWar‌ #Trump #PMModi #Putin #Xi #India

SonaSelection India – Interesting IPO given Textile theme has picked up wit UK and other FTAs

Transforming Into An Integrated Textile Platform
Sona Selection is moving beyond a processing and trading-led model towards a vertically integrated textile business spanning yarn manufacturing, technical textiles and RMG (ready-made garments).

Strong Manufacturing-Led Transformation
Manufacturing contribution increased from 11.28% of revenue in FY24 to 81.50% in FY26, indicating a structural shift towards higher-value, controlled manufacturing operations.

Strong Financial Growth Track Record
Between FY24-FY26:
Revenue grew at 106.71% CAGR
EBITDA grew at 72.51% CAGR
PAT grew at 61.19% CAGR
Growth has been supported by increased manufacturing contribution and operational scale-up.

Moving Up The Textile Value Chain
The company is expanding from yarn → technical textiles → RMG, enabling higher value addition, better customer proximity and improved margin potential.

Entry Into Technical Textiles Segment
Signed an MoU to enter military-grade fabric manufacturing, targeting the growing opportunity in specialised defence and industrial fabrics.

RMG Expansion To Capture More Value
Moving downstream into ready-made garments enables participation closer to the end customer and opens opportunities for higher-margin textile products.

In-House Yarn Manufacturing Readiness
Strengthening backward integration by developing internal yarn capabilities to reduce outsourcing dependence, improve quality control and enhance margins.

Focus On Cost Optimisation & Sustainability
A 1.2 MW solar plant supports lower power costs while improving operational efficiency and sustainability initiatives.
Balance Sheet Strengthening Through Debt Reduction
Planned debt repayment of around Rs. 80 crore is expected to reduce interest costs and improve financial flexibility for future expansion.

Capacity Expansion Through Productivity Capex
Planned Rs. 50 crore productivity capex focused on improving manufacturing efficiency, automation and scaling capabilities.

Sona Selection is transitioning from a traditional textile processor into an integrated, higher-value textile platform — combining manufacturing scale, technical textiles, RMG expansion and balance-sheet improvement to build a more diversified growth engine.

items.description_html:
Ather Energy: Building A Scalable EV Platform Beyond Premium Scooters

Ather is transitioning from a premium electric scooter maker into a broader EV mobility platform by expanding its product portfolio, manufacturing capacity, distribution network and software ecosystem.

Key Strategic Progress

1. Product Portfolio Expansion

Expanded beyond the core 450 platform with Rizta S (159 km) and Rizta S (161 km) variants.
Rizta has become Ather’s fastest-selling product, strengthening its presence in the family scooter segment.
Upcoming EL platform and e-bike portfolio could expand its addressable market beyond scooters.

2. Geographic Expansion

Replicated its South India success model in new markets.
Middle India market share increased from 4.1% in Q1 FY25 to 17.4% in Q4 FY26.
The company is now scaling this playbook across the rest of India through stronger retail and service presence.

3. Distribution & Service Network Scale-Up

Retail and service network doubled during FY26.
Wider footprint improves customer accessibility and supports faster adoption in new regions.

4. Manufacturing Scale-Up

Factory 3.0 development is progressing, with Phase 1 targeting 5 lakh units annual capacity.
Upon completion of both phases, combined manufacturing capacity across Hosur and Factory 3.0 is expected to reach 14.2 lakh units annually.
Increased localisation of components like transmission, electronics and painting can improve cost efficiency and supply-chain resilience.

5. Software-Led Revenue Opportunity

AtherStack Pro achieved 91% attach rate in FY26.
Software and digital services are becoming an additional revenue stream, improving customer lifetime value.

6. Margin Improvement & Operating Leverage

Gross margin, EBITDA margin and profitability improved through:
Higher operating leverage
Better cost discipline
Scale benefits

Investment Perspective
Ather’s next phase is not just about selling more scooters — it is about building a vertically integrated EV ecosystem.

The key factors to track:

EL platform adoption

Factory 3.0 ramp-up

Expansion beyond South India

Improvement in margins

Growth of software-led revenues

If execution remains strong, Ather could evolve from a niche premium EV player into a scaled EV technology company with multiple growth engines.

items.title: Ashutosh Fibre IPO : A Technical Yarn Player Moving Towards Higher-Value Products Ashutosh Fibre is an interesting play on technical textiles rather t...
items.description_html:
Ashutosh Fibre IPO : A Technical Yarn Player Moving Towards Higher-Value Products

Ashutosh Fibre is an interesting play on technical textiles rather than conventional textile demand. The company manufactures specialised yarns engineered for specific performance characteristics such as high tensile strength, flame resistance, heat resistance, chemical stability, abrasion resistance and anti-static properties.

Its products ultimately find applications across defence, protective clothing, automotive components, filtration and pollution control, geotextiles, industrial fabrics, thermal insulation, packaging and home furnishing.

Why the Business Looks Interesting

1. The biggest change is happening in the revenue mix and profitability.

Revenue from operations increased only modestly from Rs. 109.9 crore in FY24 to Rs. 117.4 crore in FY26, but EBITDA increased from Rs. 16.1 crore to Rs. 31.1 crore over the same period.

As a result:

EBITDA margin: 14.7% → 15.6% → 26.5%
PAT: Rs. 7.0 crore → Rs. 8.5 crore → Rs. 16.0 crore
PAT margin: 6.4% → 7.5% → 13.7%
ROCE: 21.0% → 16.3% → 26.3%

So FY26 growth was less about topline acceleration and more about a sharp improvement in business mix and profitability.

The most interesting development is the shift away from Indutech towards higher-growth categories.

2. What Industries Does It Serve?

Its yarn portfolio gives it exposure to several specialised applications:

Protech: Flame-retardant and heat-resistant yarns used in PPE, safety apparel and industrial thermal barriers.

Mobiltech: Friction-resistant yarns used in brake pads, clutch facings and transmission components.

Indutech: Filtration, filter cartridges, ropes, webbings and other industrial applications.

Hometech: Home furnishing textiles, carpets and filtration media.

Its broader product range includes para-aramid-based spun yarn, high-tenacity polyester, meta-aramid, FR viscose, modacrylic yarn, polypropylene yarn, stainless-steel yarn and specialised friction-spun yarns.
That creates exposure to structural themes including industrial safety, defence, automotive, pollution control and filtration, infrastructure and specialised manufacturing.

3. Capacity Is Becoming The Next Constraint

The company's main technical/synthetic yarn capacity stood at 3,750 MT in FY26, while production reached 3,619 MT.

That means utilisation has increased sharply:

FY24: 80.2%
FY25: 86.6%
FY26: 96.5%

This is important because the existing facility is approaching full utilisation precisely when newer categories such as Protech are scaling.

Ashutosh Fibre therefore plans to expand within its existing Petlad, Gujarat facility, adding compact spinning systems and high-value yarn attachments such as the Pinter Hard Core system.

Expanding within the existing facility should allow the company to leverage existing infrastructure, workforce and administrative resources — potentially making the expansion more capital-efficient.
Moving Downstream Into Modacrylic Fabrics
Another interesting strategy is forward integration.

4. Moving up in Value Chain
Ashutosh already manufactures modacrylic-based yarn used for high-performance fabrics. It now wants to move into manufacturing and selling the fabric itself.

The company has started trial production through third-party weaving and processing facilities and is targeting approximately 20,000 metres of modacrylic-based fabric sales per month.

The important part is that Ashutosh's own yarn would be consumed as the raw material.

This potentially allows it to move from being only a yarn supplier towards a higher-value finished technical textile product, improving value addition and potentially margins.

5. Exports Could Become Another Growth Lever

Exports are already meaningful:

FY24: Rs. 47.9 crore — 43.6% of revenue
FY25: Rs. 43.4 crore — 38.1%
FY26: Rs. 45.8 crore — 39.0%

The company plans to use additional capacity to target new international markets for specialised technical yarns.

Ashutosh Fibre is interesting because three transitions are happening simultaneously:

Volume → Value: Higher-value technical and performance yarns are becoming more important.

Yarn → Fabric: The company is attempting to move downstream into modacrylic technical fabrics.

Domestic + Existing Exports → Larger Global Opportunity: Nearly 40% of revenue already comes from exports, while new capacity is intended partly to deepen international penetration.

IPO coming at 12.5 PE

items.title: Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles. A key q...
items.description_html:
Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles.

A key question is — if the existing sponsor capital has already increased by nearly 20% in the last year, why does the company need to raise fresh capital from public investors to invest further in these high-risk, illiquid assets?

Interestingly, around 85% of Gaja’s income comes from management fees and carried interest, while income from sponsor commitments contributes only about 10%.

This raises a fundamental question: a significant portion of the fresh issue proceeds is being deployed toward an activity that currently contributes a relatively small share of revenue.

Moreover, carried interest is dependent on successful exits and realisation of investment gains. Until portfolio investments are monetised, the carried interest recorded in financial statements may not necessarily translate into actual cash inflows.

The key investor question is whether the additional sponsor commitments will create enough incremental value through future fee income and carry generation to justify the capital being raised

items.description_html:
If you approach equity investing with a “buy and forget until 2030” mindset, surviving over the long term can become very difficult.

Nobody knows in advance which stock will become a multibagger.

A multibagger is a journey, not a prediction made on the day of purchase.

Interestingly, some of my biggest gains came from stocks that I had not initially expected to become multibaggers.

Investing is like a sport - every position needs to be tracked, reviewed & reassessed regularly.

Every quarter, ask:
- Is the business moving in the right direction?
- Is management executing as expected?
- Does the risk-reward remain favourable?

Hold only while the investment thesis remains intact. We have seen several promising stories eventually go down the drain.

Conviction is important, but blind conviction reflects a lazy mindset.

Be practical - Finding a stock is only the beginning.

items.title: RT Dhirendra Kumar: A few weeks ago I wrote that a tool every investor can buy cannot set any investor apart. Why AI investing tools don't give invest...
items.description_html:
RT Dhirendra Kumar
A few weeks ago I wrote that a tool every investor can buy cannot set any investor apart. Why AI investing tools don't give investors an edge: https://vro.in/s229348. The line came from Vineet Nayar's new book, Humans First, Machines Second. His point is plain. AI is powerful and everyone has it. Something everyone has cannot make anyone special.
That left a question I did not answer. If the machine is common, what is uncommon?
I think the machine has taken the middle of the work and left us the two ends. It has not taken the beginning, which is deciding what question to ask. It has not taken the end, which is deciding whether the answer is any good.
Ask an AI to analyse a fund and you will get a competent analysis of that fund. It will not tell you that the reader's real problem is not this fund but whether he should be in this category at all. Knowing that comes from thirty years of reading letters from investors.
The machine will also give you ten sensible options. Picking the one that suits this reader in this market is not calculation. It is judgement, and judgement is mostly the memory of having been wrong before.
Then there is the story. The investor who sold everything in March 2020 did not lack information. He lacked a story strong enough to hold him when the fear came. Nobody gets that story from a prompt. AI can help you invent. It cannot invent.
One more thing. The machine agrees with you. Tell it you like a stock and it will find reasons to like it. What a person needs from an advisor or an editor is the opposite: someone willing to say no.
Nayar says the danger is not smarter machines but people losing faith in what only they can do. In our business, that is the risk worth worrying about.

items.title: RT Arnaud Bertrand: You can say what you want about Iran but they're definitely pretty unique in their communication: never seen a country threaten an...
items.description_html:
RT Arnaud Bertrand
You can say what you want about Iran but they're definitely pretty unique in their communication: never seen a country threaten another with a math equation before 😅

For those who didn't get it: there is a famous monetary policy formula used by the Fed called the "Taylor rule" that says a central bank's policy rate (i) should equal the neutral real rate (r*) plus target inflation (π*), plus 1.5 times the inflation gap and 0.5 times the output gap (the "i = r* + π* + 1.5(π−π*) + 0.5(y−y*)" part of Ghalibaf's formula).

Ghalibaf adds α(SOH−SOH*) and β(BEM−BEM*): SOH referring to the Strait Of Hormuz and BEM to Bab El-Mandeb. Both have positive coefficient, meaning the more those chokepoints are choked, the higher the rate the Fed would have to set to fight the resulting inflation.

In a nutshell this is Ghalibaf trolling the Fed, telling them that Iran is - in a very real way - setting American monetary policy.


محمدباقر قالیباف | MB Ghalibaf: Straits Taylor Rule:

i = r* + π* + 1.5(π−π*) + 0.5(y−y*) + α(SOH−SOH*) + β(BEM−BEM*), α,β > 0

Let’s see if a hike could open SOH or produce a single barrel :)

You can’t 25bp a chokepoint and r* isn’t neutral. It’s SOH risk premium, and We set it.

Stay unanchored !

items.title: Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20% The vaccine is not a prev...
items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

items.description_html:
Semiconductor supply chain

The semiconductor industry is not a market.
It’s a stack of monopolies.

Everyone talks about TSMC and NVIDIA.

Almost nobody talks about the companies without which neither can ship an advanced chip.

• ASML - 95% of lithography
• Tokyo Electron - 92% of coater/developers
• HOYA - 60% of mask blanks
• Shin-Etsu + SUMCO - ~55% of silicon wafers
• Ajinomoto - ~100% of ABF packaging film
• Lasertec + KLA - dominate mask inspection
• Advantest - majority of testers

Fabs are the visible part.
These companies are the actual chokepoints.

This is why “just build more fabs” is a slogan, not a strategy.

items.title: Nickel production routes Nickel isn’t one market. It’s a class divide. Batteries need Class I (>99.8%). Stainless takes Class II. Most of the world...
items.description_html:
Nickel production routes

Nickel isn’t one market. It’s a class divide.

Batteries need Class I (>99.8%). Stainless takes Class II. Most of the world’s nickel still ends up in steel and the high-purity stuff is getting harder to find.

• Sulphides feed Class I cleanly. They’re scarce and getting scarcer.

• Growth is laterite. Cheap into NPI / FeNi / stainless. Hard and expensive into battery-grade.

• Conversion exists: NPI/FeNi → matte → sulphate. HPAL on laterites. MHP/MSP or dissolved Class I into PCAM.

• MHP and matte can also be refined back into LME-deliverable Class I.

That’s why nickel doesn’t trade like copper. Two ores, two products, one metal and the battery chain sits on the tight side of the split.

items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
"It would be surprising if the Tata Sons board simply acquiesced to the RBI. Five of its six current directors were on the board in 2024 and were ostensibly against listing, without which the company would not have moved to deregister itself. The group doyen Ratan Tata was alive then and his desire to keep the holding company private is widely known. Noel Tata, who has taken Ratan’s place as chairman of the trusts and joined the Tata Sons board, is also reportedly opposed to a listing.

If the board turns course now, the obvious question is: What changed?

One possibility is the bitter internal politics that have since engulfed the group, pitting Noel Tata versus Chandrasekaran.

Another possibility is simpler: the board may not have the stomach for lengthy litigation against a powerful regulator.

Few have taken on the RBI. Veteran banker Uday Kotak did, challenging its ownership rules for banks before eventually reaching a settlement and withdrawing the case.

A court battle may not deliver Tata Sons the answer it wants either, as Parekh noted earlier. Even a successful challenge could merely result in the matter being sent back to the regulator for reconsideration."

Accel India IV cashed out Rs 317 crore, selling shares at 8.6x its average acquisition cost.

Chiratae retains exposure through its separate Growth Fund I, which holds 7%, worth about Rs 342 crore at the opening price.

The late stage investors, who entered in 2024, also booked substantial gains.

ValueQuest Scale Fund sold Rs 110 crore worth of shares at 5.2x its average acquisition cost. It retains 4%, worth about Rs 208 crore at the opening price.

Edelweiss Discovery Fund cashed out Rs 116 crore at 5.4x its average acquisition cost. It retains 7.42%, worth roughly Rs 376 crore.

#DPIAlert

items.description_html:
#DPIAlert | Peak XV continues to reap multibagger returns from Groww, while Accel is also making good returns from BlackBuck.

Groww: Peak XV has cashed out another Rs 1,756 crore from Groww, taking its total reported monetisation to nearly Rs 4,500 crore.

The firm sold roughly 1.47% on September 16 at an average price of Rs 191.5 per share.

Peak XV still holds an estimated 14.2%, worth about Rs 17,000 crore at Groww’s September 16 closing price.

Against an original investment of roughly Rs 233 crore, that translates into about 19x the invested capital already recovered in cash.

Including the remaining stake, the total value stands at about Rs 21,400 crore, or 92x overall.

BlackBuck: Accel India IV sold 27 lakh shares in BlackBuck for Rs 155.5 crore at Rs 576.05 apiece last week.

This is the latest leg of Accel’s staggered exit from the digital trucking platform. Accel India IV has now sold nearly 1.3 crore of the 2.33 crore BlackBuck shares it held before the IPO.

By my estimate, it has cashed out around Rs 600–620 crore.

It still owns about 5.7% of BlackBuck, worth nearly Rs 600 crore at the latest deal price.

Accel India IV’s realised proceeds and remaining stake together imply a return of over 8x.

items.title: RT Pratik Bhakta: Small ticket lending has predominantly become a non-bank affair. Fintechs and NBFCs account for 97% of the no.of loans and 92% of th...
items.description_html:
RT Pratik Bhakta
Small ticket lending has predominantly become a non-bank affair.

Fintechs and NBFCs account for 97% of the no.of loans and 92% of the value of loans disbursed.

Small ticket lending calls for automated processes, fraud control and low unit-cost of disbursal of the loan.

This is where fintechs are winning. But banks dominate larger ticket size lending.

In terms of volume 87% of the fintech loans are sub Rs 1 lac, while they comprise 16% of the value.

Above Rs 5lac count is at 3.8% and value at 59%.

Point to note: NPAs have improved significantly over the last few years. 90+ delinquency for fintechs has fallen to 2.7% from 4.4% a year back.

Lenders are seeing good repayments and strong recovery as well.

Source: Unlocking Enterprise Intelligence, Equifax Report released at GFF 2026

At the level of capability we’re seeing from models there will inevitably be some form of coordinated self-regulation of the industry; that’s generally a good thing. The big question will be if everyone can agree to what that is. However, the way things are headed politically there’s a chance that the labs won’t even get a say in it.

And then the bigger question yet is do all the countries participate or not. Any “slow down” hinges on broad participation, which from a game theory standpoint isn’t likely until the risks are more severe and obvious.

Expect this to be pretty messy for a while.
